'''Nancy Boyda''' (born August 2, 1955) is an American chemist and politician. She is a former [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. representative]] for {{ushr|Kansas|2|}}, serving from 2007 to 2009. On November 4, 2008, Boyda was defeated for re-election [[List of members of the United States House of Representatives who served a single term|to a second term]] by [[Kansas State Treasurer|state Treasurer]] [[Lynn Jenkins]].<ref>{{cite news |first1=David |last1=Klepper |first2=Jim |last2=Sullinger |first3=Dawn |last3=Bormann |title=Jenkins unseats Boyda; Moore, Roberts re-elected |work=Kansas City Star |date=November 4, 2008}}</ref> She was the Democratic nominee for the seat in the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas#District 2|2024 election]], where she was defeated by Republican candidate [[Derek Schmidt]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Storm |first=Alyssa |date=2024-08-07 |title=Nancy Boyda will face Republican Derek Schmidt for District 2 Congressional seat |url=https://www.ksnt.com/elections/nancy-boyda-will-face-republican-for-district-2-congressional-seat/ |access-date=2024-08-07 |website=KSNT 27 News |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Early life, education, and career ==
Boyda graduated with honors from [[William Jewell College]] in [[Liberty, Missouri]], where she received dual degrees in chemistry and education. She began her career in 1978 working as an [[analytical chemist]] and field inspector. Boyda grew up in a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] family and later became a Democrat in 2003.

== U.S. House of Representatives ==

=== Elections ===
;2004
In 2004 she ran against Republican incumbent U.S. Congressman [[Jim Ryun]] in [[Kansas's 2nd congressional district|Kansas's 2nd District]]. Boyda criticized Ryun's support for [[school vouchers]] and his lack of support for public schools. She said she had left the Republican Party because it had become too conservative. Ryun criticized her for taking part in [[protests against the Iraq War]]. Boyda spent $1.1 million on her campaign, $300,000 of it her own money. Ryun spent $1.2 million. [[George W. Bush]] carried the district 59%-39% and Ryun defeated Boyda 56%-41%. The only county Boyda had won during the election was [[Crawford County, Kansas|Crawford]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=4147|title=Our Campaigns - KS - District 02 Race - Nov 02, 2004|website=www.ourcampaigns.com}}</ref>

;2006
{{Main|2006 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas#District 2}}
Boyda challenged Ryun again in 2006. The district was low on both national parties' political radars. Boyda was helped by the successful re-election bid of [[Governor of Kansas|Governor]] [[Kathleen Sebelius]], who won 57% to 40%. Ryun was a strongly conservative Republican and the [[Republican Party of Kansas]] had been rife with infighting between conservatives and moderates; moderate Republicans seem to have defected to both Sebelius and Boyda. There was also the issue of Ryun's purchase of a [[Washington, D.C.]] townhouse from Tom DeLay associates at a price well below market value. She defeated Ryun by 51% to 47% in an [[Upset (competition)|upset]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=206936|title=Our Campaigns - KS - District 02 Race - Nov 07, 2006|website=www.ourcampaigns.com}}</ref>

;2008
{{see also|2008 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas#District 2}}
In January 2007, [[National Republican Congressional Committee]] Chairman [[Tom Cole]] announced that the NRCC intended to target Boyda in 2008. Ryun announced that he would try to get his old seat back, and Republican leaders reportedly assured him that he would win.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.wibw.com/news/headlines/6544167.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928014217/http://www.wibw.com/news/headlines/6544167.html|url-status=dead|title=WIBW News headline wibw.com|archive-date=September 28, 2007}}</ref> On April 4, 2007, State Treasurer [[Lynn Jenkins]] officially announced she would run in the Republican [[Partisan primary|primary]]. She defeated State Senator [[Dennis Pyle]] in the primary.

Boyda and Jenkins were opposed in the general election by [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian Party]] candidate Robert Garrard and [[Reform Party of the United States of America|Reform Party]] candidate Leslie Martin. Boyda announced that, unlike in 2006, she would not seek assistance from the [[Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee]] for her 2008 campaign. She said that "Kansas voters should control Kansas campaigns" and that Kansans should be able to "run our election without Washington interference".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thehill.com/news|title=Just In|website=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]]}}</ref> The National Republican Congressional Committee spent heavily on behalf of Jenkins,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.joplinglobe.com/archives/kansas-boyda-s-tactics-an-issue-in-nd-district-defeat/article_ef1214e9-0801-5e2f-ad74-70f99cb41d41.html|title = Kansas: Boyda's tactics an issue in 2nd District defeat| date=November 5, 2008 }}</ref> who defeated Boyda 51% to 46%.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ourcampaigns.com/RaceDetail.html?RaceID=336053|title=Our Campaigns - KS - District 02 Race - Nov 04, 2008|website=www.ourcampaigns.com}}</ref> In April 2009, DCCC Chairman [[Chris Van Hollen]] said that Boyda left him a message saying that she regretted turning down the organisation's assistance and asked Van Hollen to play the message to any vulnerable Democrat who was considering turning down the committee's assistance. Van Hollen said that Boyda "has been very clear about the fact that she made a mistake... she clearly felt that not participating [with the DCCC's help] was a good part of the reason she failed."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://swingstateproject.com/diary/4709/ks02-the-hard-way|title = KS-02: The Hard Way – Swing State Project| date=April 2, 2009 }}</ref>

=== Tenure ===
[[File:Nancy Boyda, official 110th Congress photo portrait.jpg|thumb|Boyda's official portrait for the 110th Congress]]
[[File:Nancy Boyda - April 2008.jpg|thumb|Nancy Boyda at a town hall meeting]]
Boyda, as a freshman, introduced a bill, {{USBill|110|H.R.|476}}, to deny pensions to members of Congress convicted of bribery, conspiracy or perjury charges. The Bill passed in the House of Representatives on January 23, 2007, by a vote of 431–0. Boyda also applied to join the House [[Blue Dog Coalition]], a caucus of conservative Democratic representatives. She was unable to join as adding her would have put the Blue Dogs over their membership limit of 47.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hearn |first1=Josephine |title=Who did the Blue Dogs bite? |url=https://www.politico.com/blogs/politico-now/2007/06/who-did-the-blue-dogs-bite-001806 |access-date=February 3, 2021 |work=[[Politico]] |date=June 14, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151221004039/https://www.politico.com/blogs/politico-now/2007/06/who-did-the-blue-dogs-bite-001806 |archive-date=December 21, 2015}}</ref>

On May 10, 2007, Boyda voted against {{USBill|110|H.R.|2237}}, a measure, "to provide for the redeployment of United States Armed Forces and defense contractors from Iraq."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://clerk.house.gov/evs/2007/roll330.xml|title=Office of the Clerk}}</ref> She continued to support gradual troop withdrawal while funding troops until they return.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www2.ljworld.com/news/2007/aug/17/boyda_confident_gradual_iraq_withdrawal/|title=Boyda confident of gradual Iraq withdrawal}}</ref>

;Armed Services Committee hearing in July 2007
Congresswoman Boyda left a congressional hearing while a retired Army general testified about US progress in Iraq. Retired Army General [[Jack Keane]] had testified that since the troop surge began, U.S. forces "are on the offensive and we have the momentum." He also said security has improved in every neighborhood and district in and around Baghdad, and that "cafes, pool halls, coffee houses that I visited are full of people". Boyda said she left the [[House Armed Services Committee]] hearing during the testimony of General Keane because "there was only so much that you could take,"  and continued to say she felt Keane's picture of the situation in Iraq was inappropriately "rosy."<ref name="cjonline.com">Hananel, Sam. [http://www.cjonline.com/stories/073107/kan_188000742.shtml "Boyda defends decision to leave Iraq hearing"]. ''[[The Associated Press]]''. ''[[The Topeka Capital-Journal]]''. July 31, 2007.</ref>

Her chief of staff Shanan Guinn said, "She was frustrated with how the administration is handling the war, that no one wants to have a real conversation about ways to move forward and our brave men and women overseas are being played like a political ping pong ball."<ref name="cjonline.com"/>

Boyda later told the ''[[Manhattan, Kansas|Manhattan (Kan.)]] Mercury'', that she did not "walk out" of the meeting. Instead, she "stepped into a little room" adjacent to the meeting for five minutes, then returned.  She hoped to draw a distinction between politely excusing herself and storming out of the room.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070927150019/http://www.themercury.com/news/article.aspx?articleId=667c7a2d9e79479c848a64f72b388eb9 "A look into growth-related needs"]. ''The Manhattan Mercury''. September 27, 2007. Archived at Wayback Machine.</ref>

== Post-congressional career ==
Following her term in Congress, Boyda was named by President [[Barack Obama]] as the [[Assistant Secretary of Defense for Reserve Affairs|Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Manpower and Personnel]] at [[The Pentagon]], and was sworn into the position on July 20, 2009.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cjonline.com/article/20090720/NEWS/307209779|title=Boyda sworn in at Pentagon|first=Tim|last=Carpenter|website=The Topeka Capital-Journal}}</ref>

== 2020 U.S. Senate campaign ==
{{Main|2020 United States Senate election in Kansas}}
It was reported in April 2019 that Boyda was exploring a candidacy for the Kansas Senate election in 2020.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.parsonssun.com/news/article_46160292-6320-11e9-a9c7-4393c4f2ae49.html|title=Boyda eyes run for U.S. Senate seat|last1=Nolting|first1=Ray|date=April 19, 2019|newspaper=Parsons Sun|access-date=April 22, 2019}}</ref> She subsequently announced her candidacy to seek the Democratic nomination on July 1, 2019.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article232140317.html|title=Boyda's back. Former congresswoman will run for Senate, sets up Dem primary battle.|last1=Lowry|first1=Bryan|date=July 1, 2019|newspaper=[[The Kansas City Star]]|access-date=July 25, 2019}}</ref> While campaigning, she argued said campaign finance practices and gerrymandering are big reasons why politicians don't "work across the aisle," and she said her campaign aims to break gridlock.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kvoe.com/news/item/44114-boyda-outlines-goals-at-emporia-stop-as-her-us-senate-campaign-takes-off|title=KVOE|last=Samples|first=Chuck|date=July 10, 2019|access-date=August 3, 2019|archive-date=August 3, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190803152219/https://www.kvoe.com/news/item/44114-boyda-outlines-goals-at-emporia-stop-as-her-us-senate-campaign-takes-off|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Boyda withdrew from the race saying she would begin a non-profit to break partisan divide as opposed to running for the Senate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article235993588.html|title=Former Rep. Nancy Boyda dropping out of Kansas Democratic primary for U.S. Senate|last=Hancock|first=Jason|date=July 10, 2019|access-date=October 11, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Potucek |first1=Rachel |title=Can a Democrat win the U.S. Senate in Kansas? |url=https://www.thepitchkc.com/can-a-democrat-win-the-u-s-senate-in-kansas/ |website=thepitchkc.com |publisher=The Pitch |access-date=February 3, 2021 |date=April 8, 2020}}</ref>

== 2024 House campaign ==
Boyda filed to run for Kansas's 2nd District for the [[2024 United States House of Representatives elections in Kansas|2024 elections]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Desrochers |first=Daniel |date=July 1, 2024 |title=Republicans have held Kansas' 2nd District for nearly 30 years. Can Democrats win it back? |url=https://www.kansascity.com/news/politics-government/article289618076.html |access-date=July 13, 2024}}</ref> She defeated Matt Kleinmann in the Democratic primary, and faced former [[Kansas Attorney General|state Attorney General]] [[Derek Schmidt]] in the general election.<ref name=":0" />

Boyda has said her priorities are bipartisan immigration reform, tax cuts for working class individuals and [[Campaign finance reform in the United States|campaign finance reform]]. Like in her 2020 Senate campaign, she has expressed her desire to try to bridge the divide among Kansans politically.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://kansasreflector.com/2024/06/03/fifteen-gop-democratic-candidates-file-to-compete-in-kansas-four-congressional-campaigns/|title=Why former U.S. Rep. Nancy Boyda is running for 2nd District 15 years after leaving office|last=Harvel|first=Jack|date=July 1, 2024|access-date=July 13, 2024}}</ref> In the general election, Boyda was defeated by Schmidt by 57,162 votes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-03 |title=2024 General Election Official Vote Totals |url=https://sos.ks.gov/elections/24elec/2024-General-Election-Official-Vote-Totals.pdf |website=Kansas Secretary of State |page=1}}</ref>

== Political positions ==
In 2007, Boyda talked with protestors during a public appearance in [[Lawrence, Kansas]] after she voted to provide additional funds for America's troops serving in the [[Iraq War]]. She explained her vote by saying she would support the troops, and "I am going to do what I can to bring those troops home as soon as possible." She continued, "It's the Republican side of the aisle that’s holding things up."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Boyda disputes protesters' claims about Iraq funding vote |url=https://www2.ljworld.com/news/2007/jul/29/boyda_disputes_protesters_claims_about_iraq_fundin/ |access-date=2024-06-16 |website=LJWorld.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2008, Boyda opposed a constitutional amendment to ban [[Same sex marriage|gay marriage]] during a debate with her general election opponent and said that lawmakers should avoid "tampering" with the [[Constitution of the United States|U.S. Constitution]], in reference to a push to amend the Constitution to ban marriage equality. During that period, she also stated, "I do believe that marriage is between a man and a woman" and voted with 39 other Democrats in 2008 for an amendment that pulled back domestic partner benefits to public employees in the [[Washington, D.C.|District of Columbia]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hanna - |first=John |title=TOPEKA - The campaigns of Democratic Rep. Nancy Boyda and Republican challenger Lynn Jenkins continued Thursday to spar over Jenkins' stance on the federal minimum wage. |url=https://www.hutchnews.com/story/news/2008/10/02/topeka-campaigns-democratic-rep-nancy/20852242007/ |access-date=2024-06-16 |website=The Hutchinson News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>Office of the Clerk, U.S. House of Representatives. (2007, June 28). Roll Call 603 | Bill Number: H.R. 2829. Retrieved from https://clerk.house.gov/Votes/2007603</ref>

During her 2024 campaign, Boyda expressed strong support for [[LGBTQIA rights]], including [[marriage equality]], laws that protect the community from employment discrimination, housing and public accommodation discrimination and equal access to health care. She also shared that she is the parent of a gay son and is concerned with bullying and violence toward LGBTQIA people saying, "I am deeply concerned with increased bullying and violence toward the community. If elected, I will consistently vote to respect and protect the right to privacy no matter what our current activist Supreme Court does."<ref>{{Cite web |title=BoydaForCongress.com/home-page/issues |url=https://boydaforcongress.com/home-page/issues/ |access-date=2024-06-19 |website=Welcome |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Boyda was married to Steve Boyda, a [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] veteran and police officer. She has two children and one granddaughter. She lives on a small farm outside of [[Baldwin City, Kansas]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.cjonline.com/news/20190423/former-us-rep-nancy-boyda-considers-campaign-for-kansas-seat-in-us-senate|title=Former US Rep. Nancy Boyda considers campaign for Kansas seat in US Senate|last=Tim|first=Carpenter|date=April 23, 2019|work=Topeka Capital-Journal|access-date=August 4, 2019}}</ref>
